sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: following-time rules, hydroplaning speeds, snow tires versus chains, ABS versus conventional brakes, and drowsy-driving and visibility details
Confusable pairs among following-distance, braking and bad-weather rules, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec08-R01 | anchor: A06
The three-seconds-plus rule calls for at least three seconds behind the vehicle ahead in normal conditions, and the interval rises to four or more seconds in bad weather. [A06]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable three versus four seconds.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-R02 | anchor: A08
Hydroplaning can begin at about 35 mph, but above 55 mph the tires may leave the road surface altogether. [A08]
Why it matters: group wet roads; confusable start of hydroplaning versus full loss of contact.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-R03 | anchor: A10
With ABS on snow and ice, keep a foot on the brake and never pump, but with conventional brakes that lock, release and reapply with gradually less pressure. [A10]
Why it matters: group winter braking; confusable ABS versus conventional brakes.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-R04 | anchor: A10
Snow tires help with starting, steering and stopping in snow but do not grip well on ice, whereas tire chains give the best traction on ice and in hard-packed or deep snow. [A10]
Why it matters: group winter traction; confusable snow tires versus chains.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-R05 | anchor: A05
The car-length rule of thumb is one length, roughly 20 feet, for every 10 mph, although the manual admits no following-distance rule is perfect. [A05]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable car lengths versus seconds.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec08-R06 | anchor: A01
Drivers who are angry or excited should take time to cool off before driving, because emotions strongly affect driving ability. [A01]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-R07 | anchor: A01
Some people assume driving slower than other vehicles is safer, but keeping up with the flow of traffic helps keep the road safe for everyone. [A01]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; misconception slower is always safer.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-R08 | anchor: A01
A right turn on red still requires a full stop and yielding to traffic and pedestrians, and an incomplete stop counts among the dangers of ignoring traffic control devices. [A01]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-R09 | anchor: A02
Road rage happens when drivers lose their temper over a traffic disturbance, and it shows up as running stop signs and red lights, speeding, tailgating, weaving, illegal passing on the right, gestures, screaming, honking or flashing high beams. [A02]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec08-R10 | anchor: A02
New Jersey runs specially trained enforcement patrols as part of its campaign against road rage. [A02]
Why it matters: group aggressive driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec08-R11 | anchor: A04
Always stay in the lane that shows the direction you intend to turn. [A04]
Why it matters: group communicating; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec08-R12 | anchor: A04
Be patient in town or city traffic, avoid quick turns or lane changes, and switch on the emergency flashers whenever you must pull off the road. [A04]
Why it matters: group communicating; difficulty low.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec08-R13 | anchor: A05
Keep space on all sides of the vehicle, stay in the middle of the lane, and make sure there is room ahead to stop or pass safely. [A05]
Why it matters: group following distance; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec08-R14 | anchor: A06
The time and distance guidelines assume the best driving conditions, and practicing good following distance helps you stop safely and smoothly if the vehicle ahead stops. [A06]
Why it matters: group following distance; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-R15 | anchor: A06
Know the condition of your brakes, test them often and allow more following distance whenever road conditions are poor, especially on wet, snowy or icy roads. [A06]
Why it matters: group following distance; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-R16 | anchor: A07
In the manual's minimum following distance table, gravel calls for the same car lengths as wet pavement: 4 at 20 mph, 6 at 30 mph, 8 at 40 mph and 10 at 50 mph. [A07]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable gravel equals wet pavement.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-R17 | anchor: A07
Pass or change lanes only when necessary, only if it can be done without speeding, and only where signs and pavement markings allow it. [A07]
Why it matters: group passing; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-R18 | anchor: A08
While a vehicle is hydroplaning, even a wind gust, a shift in the level of the road or a gentle turn can start a skid. [A08]
Why it matters: group wet roads; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-R19 | anchor: A09
Winter brings extra dangers such as longer darkness, fog, rain, snow, sleet and ice, and the vehicle should carry the proper type of windshield washer fluid. [A09]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec08-R20 | anchor: A09
To judge how slippery a snowy or icy road is, brake gently while driving slowly, which also shows how fast you can go and still stop safely. [A09]
Why it matters: group winter driving; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec08-R21 | anchor: A10
Idling for more than three consecutive minutes is prohibited, with exceptions that include vehicles stopped in traffic, being repaired or waiting for inspection, emergency vehicles in emergencies, and buses loading or unloading passengers. [A10]
Why it matters: group winter driving; confusable idling limit versus its exceptions.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-R22 | anchor: A10
If the defroster stops working in freezing rain or snow, stop safely, close the windows and let the heater warm them. [A10]
Why it matters: group visibility; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-R23 | anchor: A10
Against sun glare, set the visors to shade your eyes without blocking the road, hold the wheel firmly, slow down and watch the lane markings. [A10]
Why it matters: group visibility; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-R24 | anchor: A10
Before starting in frost or ice, scrape and wipe every window and turn on the defroster. [A10]
Why it matters: group visibility; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]
